item.title: Visit charts path to more stability in ties
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-28
Visit charts path to more stability in ties Xi's trip yields eight deliverables and understandings for Sino-US relations President Xi Jinping returned to Beijing on Saturday after a journey across the Pacific that yielded eight deliverables and understandings between China and the United States, ranging from reciprocal tariff reductions and an artificial intelligence dialogue to counternarcotics cooperation and giant panda exchanges. The three-day state visit was described by Foreign Minister Wang Yi during a news briefing in Washington, DC, upon the conclusion of the trip, as "historic and of landmark significance". It built on the momentum of Xi's meeting with US President Donald Trump in Beijing in May and led to new progress in a constructive relationship of strategic stability between the world's two largest economies, Wang said. A central political outcome was the leaders' agreement to build "a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity", Wang said, noting that it further enriched the substance of the vision they set out in Beijing. Respect means respecting each other's sovereignty and territorial integrity, respecting each country's choice of social system and development path, and respecting the other side's core interests and major concerns, Wang said. Fairness, Wang continued, means pursuing mutually beneficial cooperation and handling differences through consultation, rejecting a zero-sum game in which one side's gain comes at the expense of the other's, and not seeking unilateral absolute advantage. Reciprocity means that the two countries are equal in sovereignty, that neither side stands above the other, that neither engages in hegemonic nor bullying behavior, that each side's concerns are addressed on an equal basis, and that cooperation across various fields develops in a balanced manner, Wang said. Head-of-state diplomacy has been the anchor of the relationship, Wang said. Since Trump returned to office, the two presidents have met three times, spoken by telephone five times and exchanged letters on multiple occasions, developing a pattern of interaction based on mutual respect and sincerity, he said. During a tea chat at the White House on Friday, Xi said the future of China-US relations is bright, and that it reflects the trend of history, although the road ahead is often winding with difficulties and challenges. Trump described the visit as "very, very productive", according to media reports. "A lot of very positive things happened," he said. "Great things for both countries." Wang said the leaders agreed that political and diplomatic channels should play a coordinating role, while their militaries should maintain regular dialogue and departments responsible for trade, finance, law enforcement and people-to-people exchanges should strengthen their contacts. Expanding cooperation According to the list of eight deliverables and understandings released by the Chinese side, the two heads of state endorsed the work of the bilateral economic and trade consultation mechanism and instructed their teams to implement the latest results. These included establishing and taking forward the Board of Trade and other mechanisms, an arrangement for $30 billion in reciprocal tariff reductions, and an extension of the outcomes of the Kuala Lumpur economic and trade consultations. Wang said that the new joint arrangement reached before the visit also covered an investment board and an agricultural working group. The measures would help stabilize economic ties and market confidence, benefiting businesses, ordinary people and the global economy, Wang said. During his talks with Trump, Xi said that cooperation is a two-way street: a stable China-US economic and trade relationship requires both expanding the list of cooperation and shortening the list of problems. "Three meetings between the two leaders in less than a year is a positive sign," said Gene Seroka, executive director of the Port of Los Angeles, noting that continued dialogue could help businesses make long-term decisions. "Businesses and supply chains are looking for greater stability in trade policy so they can plan with longer time horizons," he said. Building bridges In the US, Xi announced that China would invite 100,000 young Americans to visit for exchanges and studies over the next five years. Wang said the announcement followed the completion, two-and-a-half years ahead of schedule, of the earlier initiative to welcome 50,000 young Americans within five years. Jeffery Sullivan, an athletics director at Montgomery County Public Schools in Maryland, said that this could allow substantially more American students to experience China firsthand. "I think this will open doors for many students to learn and experience Chinese culture, while building countless friendships along the way," Sullivan said. Xi also announced that the giant pandas Ping Ping and Fu Shuang will soon arrive at Zoo Atlanta. The pandas arrived in Atlanta on Sunday. The visit also featured what Wang called "Chinese rose diplomacy". After Trump admired Chinese roses of different colors during his visit to the Zhongnanhai leadership compound in Beijing in May, the flowers traveled across the Pacific to the White House several months later, becoming a new symbol of friendship, Wang said. Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, also visited the US National Archives with Trump and his wife, Melania Trump, on Friday, an occasion that Wang said echoed the presidents' visit to Beijing's Temple of Heaven in May in showing respect for each other's history and culture. He said the two countries have different cultural traditions and social systems, but differences do not necessarily lead to confrontation, but can provide a broad space for exchanges and mutual learning. On Thursday, Peng and Melania visited the National Museum of Asian Art and watched American teenagers sing Chinese songs, including Jasmine Flower. Wang said the China-US relationship needs both engagement between the heads of state and closer connections between ordinary people, with broader opportunities for cooperation in education, culture, tourism, sports and youth exchanges. Shared responsibilities Wang said the global significance of China-US relations had become more pronounced amid international turbulence and uncertainty. Constructive interaction between the two countries is indispensable to addressing global challenges and easing tensions in regional hotspots, he said. Speaking at the arrival ceremony at the White House, Xi said that while China-US cooperation may not solve every problem in the world, many world problems would be hard to solve without it. The two sides agreed to establish a China-US AI Dialogue covering the technology's risks and benefits, with the next exchange scheduled for November, as well as a bilateral communication channel for AI incidents. In his talks with Trump, Xi called for continued dialogue to prevent AI misuse and abuse, keep the technology under human control and ensure that it serves human progress. Arthur Dong, a professor at Georgetown University's McDonough School of Business in Washington, DC, said that decisions made by the two countries have consequences well beyond their borders. "The potential for global stability or instability very much resides in the hands of these two leaders," he said. Xu Yifan in Washington, DC, Belinda Robinson and Zhang Minlu in New York contributed to this story.

item.title: Nation mourns death of singer, mentor Liu Huan
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-28
For decades, Liu Huan's melodic voice was a familiar soundtrack across China. It could fill a stadium, carry a national celebration or rise from the soundtrack of a television drama. Liu, one of China's best-known singer-songwriters and music educators, died in Shanghai on Friday morning at the age of 63. The news was announced the following day by the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing, where Liu taught for more than three decades. Born in Tianjin in 1963, Liu studied French literature at the University of International Relations in Beijing from 1981 to 1985. He joined UIBE in 1991, where he taught Western music history and later became an associate professor. He retired in 2023. His university obituary described him first as a retired teacher and then as a household name in music — a pairing that perhaps best captured the two sides of his life. His death has sparked an outpouring of grief and remembrance. On Saturday, singer Na Ying paid tribute to Liu during a concert in Chengdu, Sichuan province, singing Crescent Moon, one of his best-known songs. "My mentor and friend, Liu Huan, who made an enormous contribution to and helped advance Chinese pop music, has left us," she told the audience. "I want to sing a song he once performed to pay tribute to him." Chinese director Zhang Yimou also mourned Liu through his studio's official Weibo account. "Upon learning of Liu Huan's passing, I cannot help but feel saddened. You and Me continues to be sung, while its sound and spirit will forever remain at the Bird's Nest," the post said. Liu performed You and Me, the theme song of the 2008 Beijing Olympics, alongside British soprano Sarah Brightman at the opening ceremony on Aug 8, which was held at Beijing National Stadium, famously known as the Bird's Nest. Composed by Chen Qigang, the song was performed atop a giant globe before a global TV audience and became one of the defining musical moments of the Games. Liu first rose to prominence in the 1980s with songs including The Sun in My Heart and Young Aspiration Knows No Sorrow, before becoming closely associated with some of China's most popular TV dramas. His rich, resonant voice became particularly recognizable through songs such as Time and Time Again, the theme song of the 1993 hit TV drama show A Native of Beijing in New York, and the Heroes' Song, from the 1998 TV adaptation of the Water Margin. His music also became part of some of the country's most significant cultural moments. In 1990, he performed Mighty Winds of Asia with singer Wei Wei for the Beijing Asian Games. In 2014, he sang La Vie en Rose with French actress Sophie Marceau at the CCTV Spring Festival Gala. His work for television also included Flying Phoenix, associated with the hit 2011 drama Empresses in the Palace. As a mentor, Liu helped bring a new generation of singers and songwriters to a national audience. In 2012, he accepted the invitation to become a mentor on The Voice of China. Among the young singers he supported was Jike Junyi, an ethnic Yi singer. Fourteen years later, Jike Junyi remembered how Liu Huan's decision to turn his chair toward her, signaling his recognition of her performance and giving her a chance to join his team, changed her life. "Your turning around completely changed the fate of a little girl," she wrote after his death on her Weibo account, which has over 16 million followers. "She stumbled and staggered her way to today. It was you who lifted up the life of a little girl." Liu's commitment to nurturing original music became even clearer in 2014, when he served as a mentor on Sing My Song, a program devoted to original compositions. The show brought then little-known singers, including Zhao Lei and Su Yunying, into stardom. In 2019, he established the Liu Huan Original Music Fund, donating 20 million yuan ($2.9 million) of his own money to support young Chinese-language singer-songwriters. On Dec 31, 2025, Liu appeared as the closing act at the Bilibili New Year's Eve Gala in Shanghai — his final major public performance. On a freezing outdoor stage, he sang I Wish to Be Immortal, a song associated with the TV series Journey to the West: The Sequel, and Time and Time Again. Despite the biting cold, Liu sang as young people in the audience joined him.

item.title: Two giant pandas arrive in Atlanta for 10-year stay
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-28
Two giant pandas arrive in Atlanta for 10-year stay A chartered cargo plane carrying a pair of Chinese giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, landed in Atlanta in the southeastern United States on Sunday morning. The two giant pandas are expected to stay at Zoo Atlanta for 10 years, according to an agreement between the zoo and the China Wildlife Conservation Association. The two pandas, both born in 2020, departed Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport in Sichuan province at 2:55 am on Sunday, after a farewell ceremony held by the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding, according to a media release by the National Forestry and Grassland Administration. During his just-concluded state visit to the US, President Xi Jinping announced that the two giant pandas would arrive at their new home in Zoo Atlanta in a few days. The media release mentioned the thorough preparations that were undertaken for the giant panda duo's trans-Pacific journey and life in the US. Two teams of Chinese veterinarians and keepers traveled to Zoo Atlanta in advance to make necessary preparations. They will stay at the zoo throughout the quarantine period to care for the pandas and help them adapt to their new surroundings through acclimation and behavioral training. Ping Ping, a sturdy agile male, and Fu Shuang, a vivacious female, underwent transport acclimation training to help them deal with possible anxiety and stress during the long flight. To ensure their safety and comfort during the flight, the Chinese team created a detailed transportation plan and arranged ample supplies of fresh bamboo shoots, bamboos, apples and emergency medications. Senior veterinarians and keepers from the US accompanied the pandas on the flight, monitoring their health in real time and attending to their dietary and other needs throughout the journey, the release revealed. Since December 2025, Chinese experts and Zoo Atlanta personnel have held multiple online and in-person meetings to discuss upgrades to the zoo's facilities to accommodate the two giant pandas. Acting on guidance from Chinese experts regarding facilities and equipment, husbandry and management, and food supplies and healthcare, Zoo Atlanta carried out extensive renovations in its panda enclosure. Chinese experts conducted an on-site inspection and acceptance check of the upgraded facilities in mid-September. The upgraded facilities boast a significantly larger indoor exhibit area, together with new features including climbing structures, rock platforms and a pool. The monitoring system of the zoo has also been upgraded so that it can provide more comprehensive real-time information on conditions inside and outside the enclosures. With Atlanta's climate being similar to that of Chengdu, the zoo can source a variety of edible bamboo locally, harvested fresh all year round, to fully meet the needs of the two pandas. Giant panda ties between China and the US date back decades. Following the visit of then US president Richard Nixon to China in February 1972, two giant pandas were sent to the US in April that year. Zoo Atlanta previously hosted pandas from China for a quarter of a century starting in 1999, but it has not had any since 2024. Chinese conservation institutions and Zoo Atlanta have long collaborated on panda conservation. Together, the two sides have carried out more than 30 research projects and published over 50 academic papers, achieving multiple technological breakthroughs in giant panda breeding and cub rearing, behavioral studies, and disease prevention and control. Through their cooperation, the two sides have successfully bred seven pandas, representing a high level of achievement in international panda breeding cooperation.

item.title: Chinese tech firms target walking-assist wearables
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-28
As Ren He, 52, stood at the foot of more than 1,400 steps on the western slope of Changbai Mountain in Northeast China's Jilin province last month, his routine cycling gave him the confidence that he could make it to the top. "But I also knew the muscle soreness would affect my trip the next day," he said. Fortunately, for just 88 yuan ($13.1), he could scan a QR code, open a locker and take out a device that claimed to "cut physical exertion by 40 percent". Despite having seen short videos about exoskeletons being used by the military and in labor-intensive jobs, this was the first time Ren had seen one in real life. With a staff member helping him into the device, Ren immediately felt the power assistance as he walked. "I climbed to the top at Tianchi Lake, and came back down. The whole round trip felt surprisingly easy, and the next day I had no backache or leg pain," Ren recalled. Such exoskeleton rental stations have been emerging at many scenic spots across the country, including the Badaling section of the Great Wall in Beijing, Taishan Mountain in Shandong province and Huashan Mountain in Shaanxi province, with rental costs ranging from 80 to 200 yuan. Ren noted that the experience underlines how technological progress can bring convenience to everyday life at an affordable cost. As a Beijing native, he sees the device's potential, noting that the city has many old residential buildings without elevators, where older residents who struggle with stairs could rely on the device for support. Such equipment was once primarily the preserve of the military, the industrial sector and medical rehabilitation. However, with advances in lightweight motors, artificial intelligence systems and wearable technologies, assisted outdoor mobility has emerged as a promising new field. And Chinese tech companies are leading the way. Founded in 2021, Hypershell is a global pioneer in the sector. With the release of its Hypershell X series in 2024, the company was among the first to achieve mass production and commercialization of consumer-grade exoskeletons. A recent surge has seen more domestic tech enterprises and outdoor sports brands jump onto the exoskeleton bandwagon. On Sept 22, ULS Robotics released Viatrix X, its new-generation 2.58-kilogram exoskeleton, which is designed for outdoor exploration. Xie Gongjin, president of marketing at the company, said exoskeletons have become lighter and more comfortable, while deeper AI integration enables more precise human-machine collaboration. "As the robotics industry chain matures and core components are mass-produced, the price of consumer-grade exoskeletons has fallen into a range the general public can accept," he said. Unlike industrial and medical exoskeletons, he added, outdoor exoskeletons target ordinary users and have huge market potential. "Complex, open mountain and wild environments are where exoskeleton technology can create the greatest value," he said. Industrial exoskeletons, Xie said, are designed for standardized, repetitive tasks within a limited range of motion, such as bending, lifting and carrying. Outdoor use requires a dynamic system that responds to human movement in real time, he added. Liu Yufeng, a trail running enthusiast in Chongqing, recently tried out an exoskeleton device from Chinese outdoor brand Toread during a running-club event in Wulong district. "After putting on the exoskeleton, I found the assistance was especially noticeable when going up stairs, and on the descent I could feel the machine cushioning my steps," he said. The 36-year-old regularly runs 150 to 200 kilometers a month, but as fit as he is, he still occasionally feels knee fatigue and reduced stability. "As I get older, my athletic ability declines and my muscles weaken. If I want to stay comfortable and safe in the mountains, I would consider using an exoskeleton," he said.

item.title: China's northernmost high-speed rail starts service
item.description:

China's northernmost high-speed railway starts service Share - WeChat
HARBIN -- China's northernmost high-speed railway, running through a region of discontinuous permafrost in Northeast China's Heilongjiang province, officially entered service on Monday. The first train departed from the forest city of Yichun at 10:26 am and is scheduled to arrive in Harbin, the provincial capital, at 12:05 pm, according to China Railway Harbin Group Co., Ltd.

item.title: 'Shoestring crew' puts drama and passion back into videos
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-28
As AI-generated short videos proliferate online, a self-described "shoestring crew" in Xi'an, Shaanxi province, has taken a different path, adapting stories from Chinese-language textbooks into live-action short dramas. Its Douyin account, @Haojiahuo, has more than 5.06 million followers, and some of its videos are now shown in primary and secondary school classrooms. The team started in mid-2024 with four young novices and 30,000 yuan ($4,470) in startup capital. None of them knew how a production crew should operate, nor did they have formal film or television training. But they studied historical material for content, polished scripts and insisted on shooting on location. The word "haojiahuo" is a homophone of a Shaanxi dialect expression roughly meaning "good heavens" or "wow". It is a plain and down-to-earth expression. "At first, we just hoped that after watching our videos, viewers would say, 'Good heavens! Well made!'" said Zhang Shuaipeng, the director and writer. The inspiration for their productions came from his favorite China Central Television program China in the Classics. "I realized historical stories could be performed with powerful details," said Zhang, who studied marketing. Over a meal, he recruited Zhang Zhiyuan as the lead actor because he had taken a half-year acting elective in university. Also joining the team were a producer nicknamed "Big Beard", who prefers not to give his real name, and cinematographer Tang Dekai, a new graduate. The four hit it off and decided to start turning Chinese-language textbooks into live-action dramas. The subject matter varied, but some of the stories were based on real historical events or characters. In November 2024, their first adaptation, Kong Yiji, the story of a failed scholar, was released. The response was lukewarm. Viewers were blunt in pointing out the problems. Zhang still remembers comments such as: "Makeup and costumes look like an old-fashioned stage play", "Stiff acting", "Continuity errors". At the time, the team lacked video-making experience and had rudimentary equipment. Looking back, Zhang concedes the result was rough. The shoot was completed at a restaurant in Xi'an, with nearby villagers used as extras. The story by the famous writer Lu Xun takes place in a small town in Jiangnan, the region south of the Yangtze River. But the people in their video spoke with strong Shaanxi accents. There was, however, some positive feedback. Many viewers said they saw their own lives in the video and shared the protagonists' emotions such as helplessness and self-mockery. Some teachers and parents told the team they had played the video for their students and children.

item.title: A red thread runs through it
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-28
Editor's note: China Daily reporters leverage local expertise to devise diverse itineraries that showcase a blend of historical landmarks and natural wonders in highly recommended cities and sites, offering practical guidance to experience the country. There are journeys that take you to a destination, and there are journeys that take you into history. The Long March is both. Ninety years after the Red Army completed its epic trek, travelers are retracing its route across Jiangxi, Hunan, Guizhou, Sichuan, Gansu and other provinces and regions, crossing mountains, grasslands and historic sites along a route that has become one of China's most significant red tourism trails. The Long March (1934-36) by the Red Army, the predecessor of the People's Liberation Army, was launched by multiple forces from different revolutionary base areas across southern China, with the main force embarking from Jiangxi. After traversing about 12,500 kilometers, the main forces eventually joined up in northwestern China, including Jiangtaibu, in today's Ningxia Hui autonomous region, and Huining, Gansu, in October 1936. Pursued by more than one million enemy troops, the Red Army endured extraordinary hardships along the way. Today, the route offers travelers a different way to encounter that history — not simply by reading about it, but by walking through the landscapes where it unfolded. From Guizhou to Sichuan and Gansu, each stop along the way reveals a different chapter of the Long March. In Guizhou, visitors can explore the site of the Zunyi Conference, where a pivotal meeting in the history of the Red Army took place — a turning point that saved the revolutionary cause and established Mao Zedong's leadership at a critical moment when the Red Army was facing crises. In Sichuan, travelers climb snowcapped mountains and cross marshy grasslands, following routes that evoke the arduous conditions faced by Red Army soldiers. In Gansu, visitors to Huining county can stand beneath the memorial tower marking the meeting of the three main Red Army forces and learn about the events that brought the Long March to its final stage. Experiences like these turn history from words on a page into something tangible — something encountered through places, landscapes and personal experience. Today, Long March-themed tourism is also finding new ways to engage younger travelers. Hiking routes, live reenactments and virtual reality experiences invite visitors to retrace sections of the journey and encounter its history in more immersive ways. As new generations retrace those historic footsteps, the stories and memories associated with the journey continue to find new life. With the nationwide Long March National Cultural Park project launched in 2019, the revolution's legacy becomes a source of courage and inspiration for the Long March of our new era.

item.title: Advanced manufacturing pushed
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-28
Advanced manufacturing pushed No longer simply about humanoid robots or spacecraft, but about remaking system At a limestone mine run by Anhui Conch Cement, a massive dump truck winds along a road with nobody behind the wheel. Guided by the Beidou Navigation Satellite System, 5G and laser radar, it can drive, park, unload and take dispatch orders on its own, while one worker in a control room can oversee five vehicles at once. The driverless mine is a small but telling example of what China increasingly means by "advanced manufacturing". It is no longer simply about making electric vehicles, humanoid robots or spacecraft, but about remaking the industrial system itself — using artificial intelligence, data and green technologies to upgrade everything from cement and steel to cars, chips and robotics. That strategy was pushed to the forefront as top Chinese leadership called for sustained efforts to expand and strengthen advanced manufacturing, and make the country's industrial chains more self-supporting and risk-resilient at a national advanced manufacturing conference in Beijing earlier this month. The emphasis is significant for the world's biggest manufacturing economy. After decades in which China built its industrial strength around enormous production capacity, infrastructure, supply chains and a vast domestic market, its next manufacturing challenge is moving deeper beneath the finished product, industry experts said.

item.title: Buckwheat noodles carry living Long March memories
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-28
Buckwheat noodles carry living Long March memories in Wuqi Share - WeChat
Came for the noodles. Stayed for the history. In Wuqi county, Shaanxi province, a veteran treated a group of visiting college students from Beijing to local lamb chopped buckwheat noodles — and with the meal came 90-year-old memories of the Long March. Some dishes come with more than flavor; they carry a living legacy. Chen Siyang, Gong Shaojun, Yao Fuxiang, Qiu Tong and Liu Yuting contributed to this story.

item.title: Hi Five China: Huaihua's bamboo breakthrough
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-28
Hi Five China: Huaihua's bamboo breakthrough In Huaihua, a mountain city in Central China, you might be surprised by what bamboo can do. Keyboards, mice and even truck bed panels can all be made from bamboo. Huaihua is home to more than 112,000 hectares of bamboo forest and some 310 million bamboo plants. For at least 7,000 years, people here have lived and worked with bamboo. Today, that long tradition is taking on new possibilities. In 2025, "bamboo as a substitute for plastic" was included in China's 15th Five-Year Plan, which calls for accelerating the development of bamboo-based alternatives to plastic. Huaihua is already putting that idea into practice. Its bamboo truck bed panels have entered the supply chains of international automakers, including Mercedes-Benz and Volvo, offering an alternative to steel. Through the Huaihua International Land Port, bamboo products reach more than 50 countries and regions. Follow China Daily reporter Yan An on the ground to see how a piece of bamboo makes its way from the mountains to the world — and how China's green development is creating benefits beyond its borders.
